turns.doctor_question: Hi, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?
turns.patient_response: I guess... they brought me in because of work. At the warehouse, I keep doing things like... well, freezing with my arms up by the forklift. It's like I have to hold the air. And I copy the beeping sounds, you know? Beep, beep, beep... and the hand signals the drivers make. I just do them over and over. And I move the boxes in these strange little patterns, even when the foreman and everyone is yelling for me to stop. They just yell so much. My cousin used to yell like that when we played video games. We played this one game with cars for hours, and he'd just scream if I crashed. I liked the blue car best, but the controller was sticky. It always smelled like orange soda. I don't drink soda anymore, though. The bubbles feel too loud.

symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient's speech exhibits tangentiality and loose associations, drifting from the foreman yelling to a cousin playing video games, a sticky controller, orange soda, and loud bubbles.
symptom_reasoning.S022: The patient describes freezing in postures, copying sounds (echolalia) and hand signals (echopraxia), and moving boxes in repetitive, strange patterns (stereotypy).

turns.doctor_question: When you do those movements or copy the beeps, is it because you feel you must do them to stop something bad from happening?
turns.patient_response: Stop something bad? No... no, I don't think so. It's not like that. I just... I just do it. Bad things just happen anyway, you know? Like when the forklift broke down last month. The mechanic came in, and he had this huge wrench. It was so shiny, it reminded me of the good silverware at my grandma's house. She used to polish it every Sunday before we ate. We always had roast beef on Sundays. I actually tried making roast beef once when I was living in the dorms, back when I was taking some classes. But my hot plate smoked up the whole room. The fire alarm went off, and it was just... so loud. Everyone had to stand outside in the parking lot in the snow. I didn't even have my boots on. My toes were freezing.

symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient's speech exhibits tangentiality and loose associations, wandering from a forklift to a shiny wrench, grandma's silverware, roast beef, a dorm fire alarm, and standing in the snow.
symptom_reasoning.S066: The patient explicitly denies performing their repetitive movements or copying sounds in order to prevent something bad from happening.

turns.doctor_question: Right before you copy the beeps or make those movements, do you feel a buildup inside, like an urge or pressure that gets better once you do it?
turns.patient_response: A buildup? Um, no... I don't feel any pressure or anything like that before I do it. It's not really an urge. It just happens. Pressure... the only pressure is the air compressor at the warehouse. They use it to fill the forklift tires, and it has this huge gauge on it with a little red needle. Red needles always remind me of compasses. My dad gave me a compass when we went camping upstate once. We slept in this green tent, but it leaked when it rained. It rained so much that weekend. The mud got absolutely everywhere, all over my sneakers. They were those white ones with the blue stripe. I tried to wash them in the sink when we got back, but the mud just stained the porcelain. The landlord was so mad about the sink. He always wore these tiny little glasses that sat right on the very end of his nose.

symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient's speech demonstrates severe tangentiality and loose associations, drifting rapidly from the concept of pressure to an air compressor, a compass, camping, mud, sneakers, a sink, and finally a landlord's glasses.

turns.doctor_question: Since you were a child, have you usually had a hard time understanding other people and making friends?
turns.patient_response: Making friends? No, I don't think it was hard. I had friends when I was little, I understood them fine. Like my friend Tyler in elementary school. We used to trade those little plastic alien figures at recess. They came in these round plastic capsules from the vending machines at the grocery store. You had to put in two quarters and turn the heavy metal knob, and it made this loud clacking sound. Clack, clack. The grocery store always smelled like bleach and old cardboard near the front doors. My mom used to get so many cardboard boxes from them when we moved. We packed everything in them, even the good plates. She wrapped the plates in newspaper so they wouldn't break, and the newspaper ink got all over my hands. It was black, but when you washed it in the sink it turned kind of grayish-purple. Purple is a weird color. You don't see a lot of purple cars on the highway.

symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient's response demonstrates tangentiality and loose associations, drifting from childhood friends to vending machines, moving boxes, newspaper ink, and eventually purple cars on the highway.

turns.doctor_question: Has anyone told you that you stay in odd postures for a long time, like holding your arms in the air without moving?
turns.patient_response: Yeah, I guess... I guess that's why they brought me in. At the warehouse, I keep doing things like freezing with my arms up by the forklift. Or I'll copy the beeping sounds it makes when it backs up, or I'll do the hand signals, or I just move the boxes in these strange little patterns. Even when everyone is yelling for me to stop, I just... keep doing it. Yelling is so loud in that warehouse because of the high ceilings. They have these huge metal rafters up there, and sometimes pigeons get inside and sit on them. Pigeons always bob their heads when they walk, it's so funny. I tried to feed one a piece of a hotdog bun once when I was sitting on a park bench. The bench had all this chipped green paint on it. Green paint always flakes off in these little curly pieces. My uncle had a green truck that did that. He drove it all the way to Florida once to see the ocean. The ocean is so salty, it makes your skin feel all tight when it dries.

symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient's speech demonstrates loose associations and tangentiality, drifting from warehouse ceilings to pigeons, a park bench, green paint, an uncle's truck, and the ocean.
symptom_reasoning.S022: The patient confirms freezing in odd postures with arms up, copying sounds and hand signals (echolalia/echopraxia), and moving boxes in strange, repetitive patterns.

turns.doctor_question: When someone moves your arm or body into a position, do you tend to stay in that exact position for a while?
turns.patient_response: No, um... I don't think anyone really moves my arms around for me. People don't usually touch me like that. Except maybe my supervisor when he grabs my shoulder to get my attention at the loading dock. He always wears these really thick leather work gloves. Leather gets so stiff when it's cold out, you know? Like if you leave it in your car overnight. I left my jacket in my car once during a snowstorm and it was basically frozen solid the next morning. My car's heater is totally busted anyway, it just blows out this freezing air and all this gray dust from the vents. Dust is actually mostly dead skin cells, which is pretty gross when you really think about it. I saw this whole documentary about dust mites on the TV in the breakroom once. The volume on that TV doesn't work, so it's just silent video of microscopic bugs and stuff crawling around. Bugs always have way too many legs. Centipedes are the worst ones.

symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient's response demonstrates severe tangentiality and loose associations, drifting rapidly from their supervisor's gloves to cold weather, a broken car heater, dust mites, and finally centipedes.

turns.doctor_question: Have people said that your face often looks blank or that you show very little emotion?
turns.patient_response: No, nobody really says that to me. I don't think my face looks blank, I mean, I smile and stuff. I see my face in the mirror every morning before work. The mirror in our bathroom has this weird smudge in the corner that won't come off, no matter how much glass cleaner I spray on it. Glass cleaner always smells so strongly of ammonia, you know? It smells exactly like the heavy-duty stuff we use at the warehouse to mop the breakroom floors. The mop bucket we have is bright yellow and one of the little plastic wheels is totally busted, so it just squeaks and drags across the linoleum. Squeak, scrape. Linoleum gets so dangerously slippery when it's wet. My roommate slipped on some wet leaves outside our apartment stairs last week and completely ruined his favorite shoes. They were these canvas sneakers with red laces. Red is the color of stop signs, but people in my neighborhood just roll right through them anyway. It's really dangerous to just ignore traffic signs like that.

symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient's speech exhibits tangentiality and loose associations, drifting from their face to a mirror smudge, glass cleaner, a mop bucket, slippery linoleum, a roommate's shoes, and finally traffic signs.
symptom_reasoning.S023: The patient explicitly denies having a blank face or showing little emotion, stating they smile and nobody tells them they look blank.

turns.doctor_question: If I gently place your arm in a new position, does it tend to stay there on its own for a while?
turns.patient_response: I... I don't know, I mean, you haven't tried to do that. I don't really think my arm would just stay there, but I guess I don't know for sure. I don't really like people touching my arms though. I got this really bad sunburn on my arms once when I fell asleep at the beach. The sand gets everywhere when you lay down on a towel. It's so hard to get sand out of your car floor mats once it's in there. I tried using those big vacuums at the car wash, the ones that take quarters? But they never have enough suction. Quarters are so heavy if you have a lot of them in your pocket. My grandpa used to collect state quarters in this big blue binder. He had almost all of them before he lost the binder when he moved to a new apartment. Moving is such a hassle, you have to pack everything into those cardboard boxes. Cardboard gives you the worst paper cuts if you're not careful. I got a paper cut on my thumb yesterday and it stung every time I washed my hands. The soap in the warehouse bathroom is that cheap pink stuff that smells like fake cherries. Cherries always have pits in them, which is annoying when you're trying to eat them. You have to spit the pits out into a napkin or something. Napkins at fast food places are always so thin, you need like ten of them just to wipe your hands.

symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient's response demonstrates severe tangentiality and loose associations, rapidly shifting topics from sunburns to sand, vacuums, quarters, moving, paper cuts, soap, cherries, and napkins without a logical flow.
symptom_reasoning.S022: The patient denies the presence of waxy flexibility (a subtype of disorganized/abnormal behavior), stating they do not think their arm would stay in place if positioned.

turns.doctor_question: Do you ever hear voices telling you to do these movements or copy the sounds?
turns.patient_response: No, um... I don't hear any voices telling me to do stuff like that. I mean, it's really loud at the warehouse anyway, so it's hard to hear people even when they're standing right next to you. The forklifts are always driving around, and they have that really high-pitched backup alarm. Beep, beep, beep. It echoes all the way up to the ceilings. The ceilings in there are just exposed corrugated metal. Metal gets so incredibly hot in the summer when the sun beats down on the roof. You could probably fry an egg on the hood of a car in that parking lot in July. I tried frying an egg on the sidewalk when I was a kid because I saw it on a cartoon, but it just made a gross, sticky mess. Eggs are so weird if you really think about it, just liquid inside a fragile little shell. I dropped a whole carton of eggs at the grocery store once and felt so bad. The floor was covered in this yellow slime. Yellow is a really intense color, like those high-visibility vests they make us wear at work. The reflective tape on mine is starting to peel off at the edges. Tape never sticks right once it gets dusty.

symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient's speech demonstrates severe tangentiality and loose associations, drifting rapidly from warehouse noise to hot metal, frying eggs, the color yellow, and dusty tape.
symptom_reasoning.S020: The patient explicitly denies experiencing auditory hallucinations, stating they do not hear any voices telling them to do things.

turns.doctor_question: Do people tell you that your speech is hard to follow or that you jump from one idea to another?
turns.patient_response: Yeah, people say that a lot, actually. Like at work, when the supervisor asks me which pallets are going on the truck, I start trying to explain the load sheet, but then my words just kind of jump... like, I'll start talking about the load sheet, and then suddenly I'm talking about my old house, and then fishing, and then these boxes from church. And by the time I'm done talking, nobody has any idea what I meant. Church always smells like old wood and those little wax candles. They have those tiny little cups for communion, they look like little shot glasses but they're made of flimsy plastic. Plastic is so bad for the ocean, you know? I saw this documentary where a sea turtle had a plastic straw stuck in its nose, and the guys on the boat had to pull it out with pliers. Pliers are really handy to have around. I keep a pair in the glovebox of my car just in case. My glovebox is mostly full of old registration papers and ketchup packets from the drive-thru. Fast food ketchup always tastes sweeter than the kind you buy in the bottle at the store. Glass bottles are so heavy to carry in grocery bags, especially if the handles on the bags start stretching out.

symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient explicitly confirms that their speech is hard to follow and that they jump from one idea to another, and their response itself demonstrates severe tangentiality and loose associations.

turns.doctor_question: Do you have beliefs that other people say are strange or not true?
turns.patient_response: I don't think so... I mean, people don't usually say my beliefs are strange. Sometimes they just don't listen to me anyway. Like the other guys at the warehouse, they just talk about sports or whatever they watched on TV. I don't really watch TV much anymore, the screen gives me a headache if I stare at it too long. My TV is one of those older flat screens, the kind with the really thick plastic border around the edge. Dust always settles right on that bottom edge, no matter how much you wipe it. I tried using those microfiber cloths, but they just sort of push the dust around instead of picking it up. You have to wash those cloths separate from your regular clothes, or else they get all these little lint balls stuck to them. Lint traps in dryers are so satisfying to clean out, you just peel it off in one big fuzzy layer. But if you forget to clean it, it's a huge fire hazard. Firefighters have to wear all that heavy gear, even in the summer. It must be so exhausting carrying all that weight around. I used to carry my backpack full of textbooks in college, and my shoulders would ache by the end of the day. Textbooks are ridiculously expensive, they make you buy a new edition every year just because they changed a couple of pictures. Pictures never look as good printed on paper as they do on a screen anyway.

symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient's response demonstrates severe tangentiality and loose associations, drifting from discussing beliefs to coworkers, TVs, dust, laundry, lint traps, firefighters, and textbooks.
symptom_reasoning.S019: The patient explicitly denies having beliefs that other people consider strange or untrue.

turns.doctor_question: For at least one month, have these movement problems and hard-to-follow speech been happening most days?
turns.patient_response: Yeah, it's been going on for a while. The confusing talking and, you know, the weird stuff I do at the warehouse... it's been happening for about six months now. Six months is a long time, half a year. That's how long it takes to get a car's oil changed, if you drive a lot. I always forget to change my oil until the little sticker on the windshield gets all faded and curled at the edges. Windshields get so dirty in the spring with all the pollen. The yellow dust just coats everything, it looks like someone dumped mustard powder all over the cars. Mustard is okay, but I prefer mayo on sandwiches. Mayo goes bad really fast if you leave it out of the fridge. Refrigerators hum so loud at night when the house is quiet. It's like this low buzzing noise that just drills into your head. Drills are super loud too, especially the heavy-duty ones they use for concrete. Concrete takes forever to dry, and if you step in it, you leave a footprint forever. I saw a dog footprint in the sidewalk once, just this perfect little paw shape right in the middle of the square. Dogs are always sniffing everything, they have such a strong sense of smell. I wonder if they can smell the pollen before it even falls from the trees. Trees look so bare in the winter without their leaves.

symptom_reasoning.S009: The patient mentions always forgetting to change their car's oil, indicating forgetfulness in daily activities.
symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient explicitly acknowledges their 'confusing talking' and demonstrates severe derailment and loose associations throughout the response, rapidly shifting topics from oil changes to mustard to concrete to dogs.
symptom_reasoning.S022: The patient confirms the doctor's question about movement problems by acknowledging the 'weird stuff' they do at the warehouse.

turns.doctor_question: Over the last six months, have you been doing worse at work than you used to?
turns.patient_response: Yeah, it's... it's definitely been worse. They actually took me off forklift duties at the warehouse because they said they can't trust me to keep things safe around me anymore. And I've fallen way behind in my community college classes, too. I even stopped showing up for my shifts at the church food bank because people kept saying they couldn't count on me. Canned food is really heavy when you have to carry a whole box of it. Some of those cans don't even have the pull-tabs on top, you have to use a manual can opener. Manual can openers always get rusty if you wash them and don't dry them right away. Rust is so hard to get off metal, you have to scrub it with steel wool or something. Steel wool feels so scratchy, it's like touching a Brillo pad. Brillo pads always have that weird blue soap dried inside them. Soap smells nice, but if you get it in your eyes, it burns so bad. I got shampoo in my eye once and it was red for the rest of the day. Red is a warning color, like stop signs and fire trucks. Fire trucks are huge, I don't know how they turn those tight corners on city streets without hitting the parked cars. Parked cars get so hot inside during the summer, it's like an oven when you first open the door.

symptom_reasoning.S004: The patient reports failing to finish schoolwork (falling behind in college classes) and failing to fulfill duties in the workplace and volunteer roles.
symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient's speech demonstrates marked tangentiality and loose associations, drifting continuously from food banks to can openers, rust, soap, fire trucks, and parked cars.
